This refutes a planar unit-distance extremal conjecture; the draft uses neither geometric incidences nor that conjectured bound.
This concerns extremal numbers of forbidden graph families; no step here reduces a conjunction of constraints to one controlling family member.

Its witness concerns Dijkstra with negative weights and a false exponential induction. This draft uses neither Dijkstra nor that recurrence, and its exponent comparisons were checked independently with exact rational arithmetic.
The edge-bijection versus graph-isomorphism error is inapplicable: no isomorphism is inferred from an edge count or edge-set bijection.
The draft never deletes a vertex from an undirected tree or assumes that such a deletion produces exactly two components.
The stone-pile counterexample targets an off-by-one geometric ancestor-count bound. No such rooted-move-tree count occurs here, and all relevant exponents were independently checked exactly.
The adjacency-matrix parity witness is irrelevant because reachability here is ordinary directed transitive closure, not positivity of a single exact-length matrix power.
This concerns arbitrary color choices in greedy planar coloring. The balanced-cut argument has no palette invariant, and every balanced partition in the finite check was tested directly.

Its missing hypothesis is that an exchanged edge is absent from a second spanning tree. Here a backward order-violating edge cannot already belong to a DAG having the maintained topological order; duplicate insertions can be discarded.
Its witness relies on an exchanged edge already belonging to both undirected spanning trees. That configuration cannot instantiate a new backward edge in the maintained DAG.

Its failure comes from orienting the endpoints of an undirected tree-path edge incorrectly. Here B and F are defined by directed ancestor and descendant closure, and the reorder proof does not make that endpoint-component inference.

results.claim: The two source-stated bounds imply total update time Õ(min{n²,m^(4/3)}). This meets Õ(n√m) when m≤n^(6/5) and when m≥n²/log^{O(1)}n; over all m it is within an Õ(n^(1/4)) factor of the target.
results.proof_sketch: The sparse-to-target ratio is m^(4/3)/(n√m)=m^(5/6)/n, so it is at most one exactly when m≤n^(6/5). The dense-to-target ratio is n/√m, which is polylogarithmic when m≥n²/log^C n. Writing m=n^a, the two available bounds cross when 4a/3=2, namely a=3/2. Before this point the ratio exponent 5a/6−1 increases; afterward 1−a/2 decreases. Both equal 1/4 at the crossing.

results.claim: Corrected balanced-cut lemma: for every order-violating insertion u→v into a DAG, either v already reaches u, so the insertion closes a cycle, or one can find equally sized sets B,F and a cut c such that F consists of the descendants of v at or left of c, B consists of the ancestors of u right of c, the stable order (L\F),B,F,(R\B) is topological after the insertion, and all |B||F| ordered pairs in B×F become newly reachable.
results.proof_sketch: Use reflexive reachability and let D be the descendants of v and A the ancestors of u. If v reaches u, report the cycle and make no cut assertion. Otherwise D and A are disjoint: a common vertex would give a v-to-u path. Sweep a cut across the old interval [v,u]. The difference |D on the left|−|A on the right| starts negative, ends positive, and increases by at most one at each position; disjointness therefore gives a zero, with nonempty equally sized F and B. In the stable reorder, a reversed old edge inside L would have type F→L\F, contradicting descendant closure; inside R it would have type R\B→B, contradicting ancestor closure; and an edge F→B would give a v-to-u path. The new edge is directed from u∈B to v∈F. Finally, every b∈B reaches every f∈F through b→…→u→v→…→f, while previously f preceded b, so no b could reach f in the old topological order.

results.claim: The balanced-cut construction gives an explicit combinatorial algorithm with total time Õ(m+n√m+A), where A is the total number of adjacency entries scanned from selected forward vertices and selected backward vertices. Consequently it attains Õ(n√m) whenever A=Õ(n√m), including sequences in which every selected forward vertex has polylogarithmic out-degree and every selected backward vertex has polylogarithmic in-degree at its expansion time.
results.proof_sketch: Apply the corrected cycle-or-cut lemma. For non-cycle violating update i, write |B_i|=|F_i|=q_i. Its q_i² product pairs become reachable for the first time. Reachability is monotone, so these products are disjoint between updates and Σq_i²≤n(n−1). If there are k≤m such updates, Cauchy–Schwarz gives Σq_i≤√(kΣq_i²)=O(n√m). Min/max heaps enumerate the two searches in topological order; non-root heap insertions are charged to scanned entries in A. A balanced sequence tree performs stable extraction and reinsertion in Õ(q_i), while edge storage and search initialization cost Õ(m). The first cycle-forming update costs at most Õ(n+A) and terminates processing. Hence the total is Õ(m+n√m+A). Under the stated directional-degree condition, A=Õ(Σq_i+n). For distinct simple edges m≤n², so m is also O(n√m).

results.claim: Full adjacency-list rescanning cannot be charged automatically to the balanced-search vertex bound: there is a DAG sequence with n=2r+2 and m=4r in which every violating update has q=1 and creates exactly one new reachability pair, yet rescanning the selected forward list costs r².
results.proof_sketch: Use initial order v,u₁,…,u_r,z,w₁,…,w_r and first insert v→w_j, z→w_j, and u_i→z for all i,j. Then insert u_i→v in increasing i. Immediately before update i, the order is u₁,…,u_(i−1),v,u_i,…,u_r,z,w₁,…,w_r, so the cut between v and u_i has F={v}, B={u_i}, and q=1. Vertex u_i already reaches z and every w_j, and it has no proper ancestor; therefore the only new proper reachability pair is (u_i,v). Nevertheless v retains its r outgoing entries, all of which an ordinary expansion rescans on each of the r updates. There are 3r initial edges and r violating insertions, while the scans total r².

final_writeup:
This remains partial progress: it does not give the requested unconditional Õ(n√m) combinatorial algorithm for arbitrary-degree insertion sequences.

The two bounds stated in the source give Õ(min{n²,m^(4/3)}). They meet the target for m≤n^(6/5) and, up to logarithms, for m near n²; their worst intermediate-density gap is Õ(n^(1/4)).

For the additional construction, discard duplicate insertions and maintain an implicit topological order in a balanced sequence tree. An insertion u→v is harmless when u precedes v. Otherwise, excluding the new edge, enumerate descendants of v in increasing topological order and ancestors of u in decreasing order, using adjacency lists and min/max heaps. If the searches certify an old v-to-u path, report that the insertion closes a cycle. Crucially, no balanced cut is asserted in this branch.

If there is no such path, pair forward and backward expansions until their frontiers cross. The corrected lemma supplies a cut c and equally sized selected sets F and B. With L and R denoting the old prefix and suffix at c, respectively, replace the order by

(L minus F), B, F, (R minus B),

preserving the old relative order within each block. Descendant closure, ancestor closure, and the absence of an old v-to-u path rule out every old edge that this block move could reverse. The inserted edge points from B to F, so the result is topological.

For update i, let q_i=|B_i|=|F_i|. Every pair in B_i×F_i becomes reachable for the first time through the new edge. Thus Σq_i²≤n(n−1), and Cauchy–Schwarz yields Σq_i=O(n√m). The heap-pop and order-maintenance work associated with selected vertices therefore already has the target total bound.

Let A be the total number of outgoing entries scanned from expanded forward vertices plus incoming entries scanned from expanded backward vertices. The explicit implementation costs Õ(m+n√m+A). It consequently proves the target under the precise additional condition A=Õ(n√m), including the stated polylogarithmic relevant-direction-degree class.

There is no unconditional bound on A in this argument. In the v,z,u_i,w_j family, every bad update has q_i=1 and creates only (u_i,v), yet repeatedly expanding v scans its same r outgoing entries r times. Therefore ordinary full-list rescanning costs r² even though n√m=Θ(r^(3/2)). This does not rule out a smarter algorithm, but it shows that the reachability-pair potential alone cannot justify the missing adjacency-access bound. The arbitrary-degree intermediate-density case, and hence the exact target, remains unresolved.
